title: Two 1.1 kg weights. Which lands first? Dropped: 0.45 s. On a pulley vs 1.0 kg: 2.07 s, 4.6x later
description:
Two weights, both 1.1 kg. Which lands first? One scene, side view, both weights on one height scale. On the left a 1.1 kg weight is held 1.00 m above a floor pad and dropped; it falls freely at g = 9.807 m/s^2 with no air drag, and the pad stops it with no bounce. On the right the same 1.1 kg weight hangs on a string over a pulley against a 1.0 kg weight: the heavy weight starts level with the dropped one, 1.00 m above its own pad, and the light weight starts on its pad on the floor. Both are held and let go at the same instant as the drop. The string is massless and inextensible and the pulley massless and frictionless (a pulley with mass is a description-only variant below), so the two weights share one speed and (m1 + m2) a = (m1 - m2) g: a = 0.1 kg x g / 2.1 kg = 0.4670 m/s^2 = g / 21 exactly, the same for any height. The pad stops the heavy weight; the light weight is then 1 m up, level with the release line, the string goes slack, and both rest until the reset. Both drops are integrated by classical RK4 at 10000 steps per second (dt = 1e-04 s) with compensated summation, the landings located by bisection inside the step, a half-step rerun as a check, against the closed forms. Shown at 1/3 speed on a 10 s cycle, 4 drops in 40 s. Deterministic, no seed.

Measured:
- the dropped weight: lands at sqrt(2 h / g) = 0.4516 s (under half a second) at 4.4288 m/s; RK4 0.451593 s (diff +0.0e+00 s against the closed form), 4516 steps; energy balance within 5.3e-15 J
- on the pulley: a = g / 21.00 = 0.4670 m/s^2; the heavy weight lands at sqrt(2 h / a) = 2.0695 s (diff +0.0e+00 s), 1.6179 s after the dropped one, 4.5826 times later (exactly sqrt(21), diff -1.8e-15), at 0.9664 m/s; 20695 steps; energy balance (m1 - m2) g x against (m1 + m2) v^2 / 2 within 3.3e-16 J
- when the dropped weight lands at 0.4516 s the heavy weight has dropped 4.762 cm (closed form a t^2 / 2 = h / 21 = 4.762 cm) at 0.2109 m/s, and the light weight has risen the same 4.8 cm
- the string holds T = 2 m1 m2 g / (m1 + m2) = 10.274 N: 0.9524 of the heavy weight's 10.788 N and 1.0476 of the light weight's 9.807 N; the net weight on the pair is 0.9807 N moving 2.1 kg
- the wrong guess: the weight difference alone, 0.1 kg of 1.1 kg, suggests a = g / 11 = 0.8915 m/s^2, which would land the heavy weight at 1.4978 s, 3.32 times the free drop; the true a is g / 21 because the 0.1 kg of net weight must get all 2.1 kg moving, 1.9091 times more mass than the difference alone counts
- the drop (real time since the release): 0.25 s: dropped 30.6 cm, 2.45 m/s; pulley side 1.5 cm, 0.117 m/s; 0.50 s: dropped on the pad; pulley side 5.8 cm, 0.234 m/s; 1.00 s: pulley side 23.4 cm, 0.467 m/s; 1.50 s: 52.5 cm, 0.701 m/s; 2.00 s: 93.4 cm, 0.934 m/s; 2.25 s: on the pad, the light weight 100 cm up
- half-step rerun (dt = 5e-05 s): the dropped weight 0.451592697 s, the heavy weight 2.069457718 s at 0.966436754 m/s, each +0.0e+00 against the full step
- a 0.2 kg uniform pulley disc (I / r^2 = 0.1 kg): a = 0.4458 m/s^2 = g / 22.00, lands at 2.1182 s, 4.69 times the free drop; a 0.5 kg disc (I / r^2 = 0.25 kg): a = 0.4173 m/s^2 = g / 23.50, 2.1892 s, 4.85 times
- 1.2 kg against 1.0 kg (massless pulley): a = g / 11.00 = 0.8915 m/s^2, 1.4978 s, 3.32 times, the string holding 10.699 N; 1.5 kg against 1.0 kg: g / 5.00 = 1.9614 m/s^2, 1.0098 s, 2.24 times, 11.768 N; 2.0 kg against 1.0 kg: g / 3.00 = 3.2690 m/s^2, 0.7822 s, 1.73 times, 13.076 N

Why: only the difference between the two weights pulls, 0.1 kg worth, but everything on the string has to speed up together, 2.1 kg in all. So the pair accelerates at 0.1 / 2.1 of g, g / 21, not the g / 11 the difference alone suggests. The dropped weight takes the whole g. Fall times scale as one over the square root of the acceleration, so the pulley side takes sqrt(21) = 4.5826 times as long for any height: 2.0695 s against 0.4516 s for 1 m. The string carries 10.274 N, less than the heavy weight (it is accelerating down) and more than the light one (it is accelerating up). A pulley with mass adds inertia and slows the pair further; a bigger difference in the weights speeds it up.
